newsitem.title: ROMANIA: OPPOSITION TO FORM NEXT ROMANIAN GOVT - EXIT POLLS.
newsitem.headline: OPPOSITION TO FORM NEXT ROMANIAN GOVT - EXIT POLLS.

text.p: Romanians appeared to overturn seven years of ex-communist rule on Sunday, rejecting President Ion Iliescu's ruling party in parliamentary elections but reserving judgment on his personal fate in a presidential race.
Exit polls showed the Democratic Convention (CDR), a grouping of 15 parties under professor Emil Constantinescu, in front with 32 to 35 percent of the vote.
Iliescu's Party of Social Democracy (PDSR), which along with its predecessor has run Romania since the 1989 fall of communism, was well back with between 22 and 25 percent.

If the exit polls are confirmed by official results, due to trickle in from late on Monday, the election will mark a stunning shift in Romanian politics. The reliability of the television-sponsored surveys was hard to gauge.
"The fact that the Convention is placed by two exit polls ahead of the PDSR shows that this autumn Sunday will change the face of Romania in a decisive way," Constantinescu told cheering supporters.
In the presidential race, the polls produced a split verdict, but it was clear Iliescu and Constantinescu would contest a run-off in two weeks.
State television put Iliescu in front with 33 percent to Constantinescu's 30. A poll on private television reversed the order, giving Constantinescu 33 to Iliescu's 31.
The outcome will disappoint the president, accused by opponents of delaying economic reform and allowing Romania to lag far behind its post-communist neighbours.
The PDSR had expected to be hit hard in the parliamentary vote but Iliescu was shocked he was not clearly in the lead in the presidential race.
"I was not in the same position as Constantinescu (of being in the opposition)," a glum Iliescu told Reuters. "I am ready for a confrontation, to give the electorate the decision."
He said he was keen for coalition talks with any partner and hinted his PDSR should form an alliance with the CDR.

But the Convention has ruled out any cooperation with Iliescu's PSDR and will presumably seek alliances with other opposition parties, especially ex-prime minister Petre Roman's Social Democrats, who have a similar programme.

But personal rivalry between the two opposition leaders blocked a post-election pact. Other potential coalition allies include a party representing the 1.6 million ethnic Hungarian minority and a grouping of liberal parties.

The Convention had based its campaign on a "Contract with the Romanian people" under which it pledged to resign within 200 days if it failed to cut taxes, improve living standards and modernise industry and farming.

Election turnout was just over 70 percent, a high figure that had been thought to favour Iliescu. Polling stations remained open until midnight (2200 GMT), three hours longer than scheduled, to cater for a late surge of voters.
Iliescu, 66, one of 16 candidates for president, has been in office since taking charge of Romania in the aftermath of the 1989 revolution that ousted dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.
Iliescu portrays his opponents as risk-takers and himself as a guarantor of stability able to avoid the more dramatic economic slide of Bulgaria and ethnic conflicts of Yugoslavia.

Reports of voting irregularities poured in throughout the day, with one Romanian watchdog organisation urging parties to lodge formal complaints. Opposition parties had said during the campaign that Iliescu's PDSR was planning mass fraud.
